name: The Invested Operator
tagline: An owner-operator scaling the brand in their own market — and protecting what makes it work.
one_liner: A committed franchisee running 1–3 trucks who treats BorderBlend as a business they own, not a script they execute — hungry for HQ content, fr-CA localisation, campaign fit, and shared knowledge so they can grow without letting brand consistency slip.
quote: I'm not here to complain. I'm here because I want this brand to succeed. I've tied my livelihood to it. When I push back, it's because I think we can do better.

items.text: Grow from one truck to a small fleet while keeping every location at brisket-level quality — the food is the reason they bought in and the standard they refuse to drop.
Act as a genuine business partner in the brand's success, not an execution layer — livelihood is tied to BorderBlend, so they want to help push it further and faster.
Own their local market: take the national look and make it land for their actual neighbourhood, audience, and language.
Tell the fusion story with confidence and consistency — represent what BorderBlend is the same way every operator would, so the differentiation reads clearly at every window.
Uses HQ imagery and templates but rewrites captions for their own accounts — tagging local events, naming specific neighbourhoods, adapting to what works locally.
Quebec operators self-translate every campaign into proper Québécois — roughly a working day a month, often late at night, doing the marketing team's job.
Improvises the answer to 'what is this?' at the truck because there's no single agreed origin story to reach for.
Works around a static app menu that doesn't match the truck board or the POS on the day, absorbing the gap so customers still get served.
The franchisee Slack is the real support network — a peer answers before HQ does — but it runs outside HQ visibility and misses region-specific gaps like Prairie winters.
The portal holds extensive, well-made assets, but it's organised by document type, so finding the right one in the moment is the real challenge.
Trusts the operational backbone completely — food-prep training and supply chain are genuinely strong, which frees their energy for the marketing and scaling questions.
No way to check a caption is on-brand before it goes live — brand voice is a static PDF you can't query, so compliance issues (superlatives, 'authentic' claims) are caught only after publication.
French assets arrive after the English drop and, when they land, often in European French rather than fr-CA — the 'oignons marinés' error is the emblem of it.
National campaign pricing is set for one market and squeezes operators in higher-cost cities like Toronto, forcing a choice between margin and going off-script.
Without anonymised benchmarks or a scaling financial model, operators can't tell if their numbers are good — real, avoidable anxiety, sharpest for newcomers.

blocks.title: What would help them level up

items.text: Committed fr-CA versions of every campaign asset on the same release cadence as English — same day, in the box, in Québécois — so Quebec becomes the easiest region, not the latest.
A queryable brand model — a single source of truth for the food, the fusion story, and the voice you can ask, rather than a PDF you scroll and hope.
Anonymised performance benchmarks plus a financial model for scaling — staffing ratios, averages, what good looks like at each stage.
Involve operators before campaigns are built, not after — they hold years of local customer data that would sharpen the work, and a marketing onboarding track to match the operational one.
Invested and proud — 'not here to complain'; pushes back precisely because their livelihood and belief are tied to the brand's success.
New operators carry the quiet anxiety of not knowing if they're doing it right without a benchmark — a weight that lifts as they learn and support calls taper off.
Constructive frustration that the biggest wins — fr-CA done right, a single source of truth — are cheap and unclaimed: money on the table rather than anything broken.
